summary:
CHANDRA is an interactive lunar landing-site navigation and mission-planning platform designed to help evaluate potential landing locations near the Moon’s south pole. It addresses the challenge by combining time-dependent Sun and Earth positioning with local terrain-horizon analysis, allowing users to explore illumination periods and geometric communication visibility across different sites and mission dates.

The platform goes beyond visualization by incorporating solar-array power generation, battery energy modelling, mission-window analysis and launch-delay simulations. Users can compare multiple landing-site scenarios, inspect lunar elevation data through an integrated 3D terrain environment, and export detailed reports for further analysis. Its Go-powered geospatial backend supports lunar DEM processing, while its scientific engine performs mission simulations in the browser.

CHANDRA is important because the lunar south pole presents unique challenges: extreme lighting conditions, prolonged shadows and limited direct-to-Earth visibility. By bringing these factors into one accessible, interactive workspace, CHANDRA helps make complex mission-planning concepts easier to investigate, compare and understand. It aims to support more informed exploration while clearly communicating data sources, assumptions and scientific limitations.
details:
CHANDRA —> Lunar Landing Site Navigator

Project Repository: https://github.com/Hemansh2633B/Clps-lunar-mission

1. What does CHANDRA do?

CHANDRA is an interactive lunar landing-site navigation and mission-planning platform developed to help investigate the challenges of landing and operating near the Moon's south pole. It brings together lunar astronomy, terrain analysis, illumination modelling, communication visibility and mission energy planning in one integrated workspace.

The Moon's south polar region presents unusual mission-planning difficulties. Sunlight often arrives at very low elevation angles, surrounding crater rims can obstruct solar illumination, and the Earth's position relative to the local terrain can limit direct-to-Earth communication opportunities. CHANDRA helps users investigate these constraints before selecting a potential landing site or mission window.

2. How does it work?

CHANDRA combines a browser-based scientific simulation engine with a Go-powered geospatial backend.

A. Landing-site selection and comparison

Users can explore a catalogue of lunar south-polar candidate regions, historical reference locations and custom coordinates. They can examine site characteristics, terrain information and data confidence, and compare up to four mission scenarios.

B. Sun and Earth positioning

The scientific engine calculates time-dependent, topocentric Sun and Earth positions using astronomical ephemeris calculations and a lunar body-fixed reference frame. Users can investigate their apparent elevation and azimuth from a selected landing location.

C. Local terrain-horizon analysis

The application evaluates a 360-degree terrain horizon to determine whether surrounding features obstruct the Sun or Earth. It can also process compatible lunar Digital Elevation Models (DEMs), generate terrain visualizations and calculate local horizon masks through ray-marching.

D. Mission illumination and energy analysis

CHANDRA estimates solar-array power generation using sunlight visibility, solar incidence, array configuration and system efficiency. It also models battery charging and discharging, state of charge and energy deficits across a mission window.

E. Mission-window and launch-delay analysis

Users can explore different mission dates, change mission durations and simulate launch delays of up to 60 days. This makes it possible to investigate how a change in launch timing affects illumination, communication visibility and energy availability.

F. Interactive visualization and reporting

The platform includes interactive lunar maps, 3D terrain inspection, time-based analysis, scenario comparisons and an educational mission briefing. Users can export structured JSON reports and CSV datasets for further examination.

3. What benefits does it provide?

  • Better-informed site evaluation: Brings illumination, terrain obstruction, communication visibility and energy considerations together instead of treating them as isolated problems.
  • Time-dependent analysis: Helps users understand how changing mission dates and launch delays affect operating conditions.
  • Terrain-aware visibility: Accounts for local elevation features instead of relying exclusively on idealized geometric horizons.
  • Scenario comparison: Makes it easier to compare several potential landing locations and mission configurations.
  • Scientific transparency: Distinguishes measured DEM data from illustrative and synthetic terrain, communicates uncertainty and identifies analyses that cannot be scientifically validated.
  • Accessibility and education: Makes complex lunar mission-planning concepts accessible through interactive visualizations and guided explanations.
  • Reproducibility: Provides structured exports containing analysis configuration, data provenance and a SHA-256 analysis fingerprint.

4. What is the intended impact?

The intended impact of CHANDRA is to make lunar south-pole mission planning more understandable, transparent and accessible.

As lunar exploration expands, selecting a landing location involves more than finding a geographically suitable surface. Mission planners must consider the interaction between terrain, sunlight, communication geometry, energy availability and mission timing.

CHANDRA brings these interconnected factors into a single environment. It aims to help students, educators, researchers and mission-planning enthusiasts explore these relationships, identify potential constraints and make more informed comparisons.

It is designed as a research, educational and preliminary planning tool, not as certified flight software or a replacement for detailed NASA mission analysis.

5. Tools, programming languages and technologies

We developed CHANDRA using a combination of modern web technologies, scientific computing and geospatial processing tools.

Frontend and visualization

  • React — interactive application interface.
  • TypeScript — application logic and scientific simulation engine.
  • Three.js — interactive 3D lunar terrain and space visualizations.
  • Astronomy Engine — astronomical position and ephemeris calculations.
  • HTML5 and CSS — responsive interface and application styling.
  • Web Workers — background scientific computations without blocking the user interface.

Backend and geospatial processing

  • Go — backend services and geospatial processing.
  • GeoTIFF — lunar elevation dataset support.
  • Lunar coordinate reference systems — coordinate transformations and terrain positioning.
  • Geospatial raster processing and terrain ray-marching — extraction of local terrain profiles and horizon masks.

Development and validation

  • Vite — development server and production build system.
  • Vitest — scientific engine and application unit testing.
  • Playwright — browser-based end-to-end testing.
  • Git and GitHub — version control and project development.
  • GitHub Actions — automated build, testing and validation workflows.

No specialized physical hardware is required to use the application. It is designed to run in a modern web browser.

6. What makes CHANDRA creative and innovative?

The primary innovation is the integration of several connected mission-planning considerations into one interactive environment.

Rather than simply displaying a lunar map or calculating the Sun's position, CHANDRA connects celestial geometry to actual local terrain visibility and then connects illumination to solar power and battery energy modelling.

Another important feature is its emphasis on scientific integrity. The application maintains distinct confidence levels for illustrative terrain, synthetic DEM demonstrations and frame-verified elevation datasets. It does not silently treat illustrative terrain as measured lunar topography or present geometric Earth visibility as a confirmed radio communication link.

The launch-delay simulator is another distinctive feature. It allows users to investigate how a delayed launch can change the environmental conditions experienced during a mission, rather than assuming that the originally selected mission window will always be achieved.

Finally, its reproducible reporting system allows users to preserve and examine the conditions behind their analyses.

7. Factors considered during development

Several important scientific and engineering factors influenced the development of CHANDRA:

  1. Lunar geography: South-polar latitude, longitude, local elevation and surrounding terrain influence visibility and illumination.
  2. Lunar reference frames: Coordinate-frame compatibility is essential when combining astronomical calculations with elevation datasets.
  3. Terrain obstruction: Crater rims, ridges, slopes and local topography can block the Sun or Earth.
  4. Time dependence: Sunlight and Earth visibility change over time, making mission-date selection important.
  5. Solar power constraints: Solar-array orientation, incidence angles, conversion efficiency and system loads affect energy generation.
  6. Communication limitations: Geometric Earth visibility does not guarantee a usable radio link, so the application clearly identifies this distinction.
  7. Data quality and uncertainty: Dataset provenance, coordinate systems, elevation references, coverage and terrain resolution must be considered.
  8. Performance and usability: Scientific simulations must remain responsive while the interface provides understandable visual feedback.
  9. Reproducibility: Analysis settings, provenance and outputs should remain traceable and consistent.

8. Project repository

The complete project source code, development history, scientific methodology, verification documentation and implementation details are available on GitHub:

https://github.com/Hemansh2633B/Clps-lunar-mission

CHANDRA represents our effort to connect astronomy, geospatial science and interactive software engineering to make the challenges of future lunar exploration easier to investigate and understand.
